cognate: Gk εὐρύς = Ved. urú- (*h₁wérHu- 'wide'); Gk πόντος = Ved. pánthā-/path- (*pónteh₁-/*pn̥th₁- 'path, passage')
drift_or_renewal: drift: the noun has shifted from 'path, crossing' (Indo-Iranian, also Lat. pons, OCS pǫtь) to 'sea' in Greek; the adjective is unchanged
shared_syntax: attributive adjective + noun in agreement (Gk dative/accusative εὐρέι πόντῳ, εὐρέα πόντον; Ved. nom./acc./loc./instr. urúḥ pánthāḥ, urúm pánthām, uraú pathí, pathā́ urúṇā), as a fixed noun-epithet pair
context: Both sides are about travel along the noun: in Homer the wide 'pontos' is what ships cross or are held on (περήσαμεν εὐρέα πόντον Od. 24.118; ἐνήσομεν εὐρέι πόντῳ 'we will launch (the ship) onto the wide sea'), in the RV the wide path is laid out for gods, chariots, the sun or the dakṣiṇā (RV 8.68.13 urúm ráthāya pánthām; RV 1.24.8 Varuṇa made a wide path for the sun; RV 10.107.1). The Greek use as 'the wide crossing' keeps the old 'passage' sense. In the corpora the pairing is above chance on both sides: Homer, εὐρύς + πόντος in one line 9 times against about 0.8 expected; RV, urú- + pánthā-/pathyā̀- in one pāda 5 times against about 0.7 expected (10 stanzas against 2.3). Because the noun has drifted in Greek, generic co-occurrence of 'wide' + 'sea' cannot account for the cognate pair: a Greek poet independently pairing 'wide' with 'sea' would not need the old 'path' word in particular.
phrase: *h₁uréHu- pónteh₁- 'wide path' > Gk εὐρὺς πόντος 'wide sea' ~ Ved. urúḥ pánthāḥ

cognate: Gk ἴς = Lat. uīs (*wiHs 'force'); Gk ἄνεμος = Lat. animus (*h₂enh₁mo- 'breath, wind')
drift_or_renewal: In Latin the dependent noun is renewed: uentus (*h₂weh₁nt-) for 'wind' (uenti uis, the context line of LucrDRN6 6.437). The exact cognate animus has drifted from 'breath, wind' to 'mind', and Latin keeps the cognate head + cognate dependent only in the psychological uis animi (LucrDRN1 1.72, 3.450, 3.159, 3.277, 3.747)
shared_syntax: head noun *wiHs + dependent genitive of the force-bearing entity, used as a periphrasis for the agent and as subject of a verb of driving or tearing (Gk διέσχισεν / ἀπώσατο / κατήγαγεν ἲς ἀνέμοιο; Lat. uenti uis uerberat ... pontum, uis ... uenti ... classis ... uerrit)
context: Storm at sea in both: Homer's ἲς ἀνέμοιο tears the sails (Od. 9.71), drives the ships off course (Od. 13.276) and carries Odysseus to Crete (Od. 19.186); Lucretius' uenti uis bursts into the sea and churns the waves (6.436-7), beats the sea and wrecks ships (1.271), sweeps a fleet across the water (5.1226). Counts: Homer ἴς + ἄνεμος in one line 5 times against 0.10 expected, a line-end formula; LASLA uis + uentus in one sentence 24 times against 2.2 expected (Lucretius only). Caveats: uis + genitive is ordinary Latin and Lucretius imitates Homer and Ennius, so the Latin may be a literary calque, not an inherited phrase. ἴς, by contrast, survives in Greek almost only in such fossil periphrases (also ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο, hom:Od. 16.476 in B-bd15c).
phrase: *wiHs h₂enh₁mosyo 'force of the wind' > Gk ἲς ἀνέμοιο ~ Lat. uenti uis (renewed) / uis animi (drifted)

cognate: Gk μέλι, -ιτος = Lat. mel, mellis (*mélit 'honey'); Gk γλυκύς/γλυκερός = Lat. dulcis (*dl̥ku-/*dleuku- 'sweet')
drift_or_renewal: none (Greek γλυκερός is a suffixed variant of γλυκύς)
shared_syntax: adjective + noun 'sweet honey' (Gk μέλιτι γλυκερῷ, Lat. dulci melle / mellis dulci liquore), and the comparison 'sweeter than honey' with honey as standard of comparison (Gk gen. μέλιτος γλυκίων Il. 1.249, 18.109; Lat. abl. melle dulci dulcior PlAsina 614)
context: In both, honey is the measure of sweetness, used of food and figuratively: of speech (Nestor's voice flows 'sweeter than honey', Il. 1.249), of anger (Il. 18.109), of a loved person (Plautus), of poetry put on the cup's rim as honey (Lucretius 1.947, 4.22). Counts: Homer μέλι + γλυκύς/γλυκερός in one line 4 of the 7 μέλι lines (expected 0.01); LASLA mel + dulcis in one line 5 times against 0.09 expected. Caveat: in each language this is just the ordinary word for 'sweet' with the ordinary word for 'honey', and 'sweeter than honey' occurs worldwide. What the two share is a Greek–Latin lexical isogloss (*dl̥ku-) inside a stock comparison, so this is at best Graeco-Italic phraseology. A parallel collocation from the other 'sweet' root, *swéh₂du- + *médʰu-, is well attested: Homer μέθυ ἡδύ (9 lines, e.g. Od. 9.162) ~ RV svā́do ... mádho (RV 1.187.2), svādóḥ ... mádhvaḥ (RV 1.84.10). The same Homeric line Od. 20.69 has ἡδέϊ οἴνῳ, with οἶνος in place of μέθυ.
phrase: *dl̥ku- mélit 'sweet honey'; 'sweeter than honey' > Gk μέλι γλυκερόν, μέλιτος γλυκίων ~ Lat. mel dulce, melle dulcior

cognate: Gk κληΐς/κλῄς, κληΐω = Lat. clāuis, claudō, claustrum (*kleh₂w- 'peg, bolt'); Gk θύραι = Lat. forēs (*dʰwer-/*dʰwor- 'door', plural for the two-leaved door); Gk πετάννυμι = Lat. pandō (*peth₂- 'spread out')
drift_or_renewal: renewal of the door word in Catullus (ianua for fores); otherwise none
shared_syntax: transitive verb derived from 'bolt' + plural 'doors' as object, for closing (Gk κλήϊσεν θύρας; Lat. clausis foribus, fores occlusae); and *peth₂- 'spread' + door or bolt, for opening wide (Gk θύρετρα ... πετάσθησαν, πεπταμένας πύλας; Lat. claustra pandite ianuae, pandite ... ianuam)
context: Closing up or throwing open the doors of a house: Philoitios bolts the courtyard doors (Od. 21.389, one of five κληΐω + θύρας lines, all in Od. 19 and 21, against 0.05 expected); Penelope's key strikes and the doors fly open (Od. 21.50). In Latin, talk through shut doors (Lucretius), doors shut to all but the lover (Plautus), and the wedding cry to open the bolts of the door for the bride (Catullus 61.76; also PlBacch 368). Counts: LASLA claudo/occludo + door 4 lines against 0.23 expected, pando + door 2 against 0.08. Caveat: these are everyday acts, and each language may have independently turned its inherited 'bolt' noun into a verb. The overlap is the same three-way lexical choice (bolt-verb, plural doors, 'spread' for opening wide) more than a fixed formula.
phrase: *kleh₂w- + *dʰwor- 'bolt the doors'; *peth₂- 'spread open (the doors)' > Gk κληΐειν θύρας, πετάννυμι θύρας/πύλας ~ Lat. claudere fores, pandere claustra/ianuam

note: All 166 bundles read in order. 4 claims: 1 medium (εὐρὺς πόντος ~ urúḥ pánthāḥ), 3 low (ἲς ἀνέμοιο ~ uenti uis/uis animi; μέλι γλυκερόν ~ mel dulce; bolting/opening doors *kleh2w-/*peth2-). Considered and rejected as generic or unsupported: cattle+sheep (gʷōws + h2owis) lists, πότνια μήτηρ ~ AVŚ 7.6.3 mātaraṃ ... patnīm (pátnī- and mātár- never share an RV stanza), father-and-mother pairs, ἔργον τε ἔπος τε (no partner).
